key_insight: The paper asks whether LLM agents can "package" their general intelligence into cheaper, reusable artifacts that handle large workloads efficiently. It introduces the idea of "bottling"—trading a bit of flexibility for much lower amortized cost while preserving useful quality.
problem_solved: Many real-world applications require running the same or very similar LLM task over millions of instances, making repeated API calls too expensive. This work tackles how agents can autonomously create task-specific solutions that reduce cost without losing too much performance.
method: Defines "bottling" as converting broad LLM capabilities into task-specific artifacts optimized for a workload.
Introduces BOTTLED, a benchmark where agents receive an unlabeled workload and must solve it under fixed cost/time constraints.
Evaluates whether agents can infer the task structure, build a cheaper solution, and balance answer quality against amortized execution cost.
impact: This is important for practitioners deploying LLMs at scale, where cost often dominates feasibility. If successful, bottling could enable faster, cheaper systems for batch processing, enterprise workflows, and repetitive decision tasks.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing: raw workload -> agent analysis -> bottled artifact -> low-cost mass execution
A trade-off chart with quality on one axis and amortized cost on the other
An icon-based comparison of per-query LLM calls versus a reusable task-specific artifact
A benchmark illustration of an unlabeled dataset/workload being turned into a solution under budget constraints
paper_title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
paper_authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Haritz Puerto, Alexander Rubinstein, Martin Gubri, Seong Joon Oh
